Bhoja
------------------------------------------
Bhojarāja or the king भोज is a well-known figure in Sanskrit literature. Belonging to the Paramāra dynasty of Māḷava (Malwa) he lived in the 11th century A.D. Some scholars assign him to the period A.

-1055. His capital was Dhārā.
The number of works attributed to him is 34. They belong to a variety of fields of knowledge that include astro-nomy, अस्त्रोलोग्य्, medicine and surgery, grammar, economics and even engineering sciences. However, it is more reasonable to believe that these works were written by the various scholars in his kingdom under his patronage.
At present, only the following five works have been found: Campū-रामायण, Rājamārtāṇḍa, Tattvaprakāśa, सरस्वती-kaṇṭhābhāraṇa and Śṛṅgāraprakāśa.
The second work, also called Bhoja-वृत्ति, is an independent commentary on the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि. It is brief but lucid. The third work is on शैविस्म्. भोज was a śaiva by faith. The last two deal with अलङ्कार or poetics and dramaturgy.

bhojana
(‘that which is eaten,’ ‘food’)
------------------------------------------
Every act of the Hindu, including those connected with his daily routine, is permeated by the spirit of religion. भोजन or taking meal is a very important part of such a daily routine.
According to Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.5.4; 6.5.1; 6.7; 7.26.2) body and मिन्द् are closely interconnected; and the ड़ोओद् eaten by us affects our मिन्द्. Since purity of ड़ोओद् is conducive to the purity of मिन्द्, great attention has to be paid to what we eat. This regulation of ड़ोओद् concerns four aspects:
quality;
quantity;
time and
place.
The ड़ोओद् should be conducive not only to health and strength but also to purity of मिन्द्. Hence, ड़ोओद् classified as sāttvic (vide Bhagavadgītā 17.7) should always be preferred.
As regards the quantity, it should be neither ‘too much,’ nor ‘too little.’ Works on the आयुर्वेद (the science of longevity or health) prescribe that half the stomach is to be filled with solid ड़ोओद्, a quarter with liquid ड़ोओद् or water, leaving the last quarter for the circulation of wind or air. Whereas young brahmacārins, who are expected to do a lot of work and study in their gurukulas, are permitted to eat sumptuously, the vānaprasthins (forest dwellers) and the saṁnyāsins (monks) have to eat very limited quantities, as much as is necessary to maintain general health and strength, necessary for spiritual pursuits.
Coming to the time, the general rule is that one should eat only when one is hungry. The time should also be adjusted to suit one’s religious practices, in a way that does not disturb their tenor. Consuming ड़ोओद् or drinks during the eclipses of the sun or the मोओन् is strictly prohibited.
Concerning the place where ड़ोओद् can be taken, physical cleanliness and pleasing sights are strongly recommended. Eating in moving vehicles or in a public place in full view of others has been prohibited. There may have been compelling reasons during those times, when these rules had been made, for such prohibition, though they are not possible to observe now-a-days.
Since purity of ड़ोओद् conduces to purity of मिन्द्, the धर्मशास्त्रस् have dealt with this subject rather in great detail.
Certain ड़ोओद् articles like garlic and onion, are ‘jātiduṣṭa’ or defective by their very nature (jāti = species, nature) and hence unfit for consumption.
Others that get polluted due to the touch of unclean hands or animals, (called ‘kriyāduṣṭa’) or belonging to the morally depraved persons (called ‘parigraha-duṣṭa’) or from the houses of those observing अशौच or ceremonial impurity (due to birth or death in that होउसे) are also prohibited.
In some of the works, it is stated that if one contemplates on the act of eating as a यज्ञ or sacrifice, he will reap great benefits (vide Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.19).
Facing east or north at the time of eating, observing silence during eating and repeating the name of God in between two morsels, restricting the ड़ोओद् of the होउसे-holder to two square meals per day, inscribing certain religious symbols below the plate or the leaf used for ड़ोओद्, showing due respect to the ड़ोओद् when it is brought for serving, keeping away small quantities of ड़ोओद् as बलि or offering to यम (the god of death) and others—these are some of the interesting side-lights in these religious works, concerning भोजन.
